title: How to Use Hermes Profiles Without Building One Noisy Assistant
excerpt: Hermes profiles separate memory, sessions, skills, identity, cron state, and gateways so AI agents can become durable roles instead of one confused generalist.
metaDescription: Learn how to use Hermes profiles for role-based agents, clean SOUL.md files, handoffs, cron ownership, and multi-agent workflows.

blocks.text: Hermes profiles are not personas. They are operating boundaries: separate configuration, memory, sessions, skills, gateway state, cron state, and identity for agents that should not think like the same assistant.
If your assistant is researcher, writer, debugger, calendar operator, and project manager at once, the problem is not prompting. The problem is shared state.

This guide turns the April 2026 Hermes profiles idea into an operator checklist. You will learn when to create a profile, what to put in SOUL.md, how to clone a working setup, and where the team usually breaks after week one.

items: **Use profiles for durable roles, not moods.** Research, writing, engineering, and orchestration deserve separate state.
**Clone a working base first.** `hermes profile create scout --clone` keeps setup work low while giving the research profile isolated memory and sessions.
**Put identity in SOUL.md and project context in AGENTS.md.** Mixing those two is how specialist agents become vague again.
**Add handoff contracts before the team grows.** A research agent should pass sourced claims, not a pile of excerpts.
**Treat cron and gateway state as production concerns.** Profiles can schedule and receive messages separately, so collisions need a shared register.

The mistake: one assistant with five jobs

A single assistant feels convenient until its memory starts carrying every job at once. The same thread holds market research, copy feedback, shell logs, calendar rules, and half-finished strategy notes.
That state leak is why broad assistants become worse as they get more useful. Every new responsibility adds context the next task has to ignore.

The common failure pattern is easy to spot: one assistant becomes the place where every task lands. It starts as convenience, then turns into context debt. The useful move is to split the assistant by responsibility before the memory, tone, and workflows blur together.
What Hermes profiles separate
Hermes 0.9.0 added profiles as isolated agent environments. A profile can split configuration, sessions, memory, skills, personality, cron state, and gateway state.

rows: A researcher can remember source quality rules without polluting a writing profile with raw notes.
A debugger can keep logs and diffs away from a client-facing writing session.
A profile can load the tools it actually needs instead of scanning every possible workflow.
Telegram or other message routes can belong to the role that should answer them.
Morning briefings, audits, and maintenance tasks can run under the profile that owns the outcome.

blocks.text: This is the difference between a name tag and an operating boundary. A name tag changes tone. A profile changes what the agent can carry over time.
A practical starter team

Start with roles, not borrowed character names. Keep Hermes as the coordinator, then add Scout for research, Scribe for writing, and Forge for building or debugging once the first two roles are already useful.

rows: A short plan, task split, final synthesis, and quality gate
Ranked claims with URLs, dates, and uncertainty notes
A structured draft with audience choices and edit notes
Diffs, commands run, failing logs, fixed tests, and residual risks

blocks.text: The first handoff to define is Scout to Scribe. Scout should send claims with sources, not a folder of raw excerpts. Scribe should send a draft and change log, not pretend the research was hers.

That small contract prevents the common week-two failure: every profile starts copying the work style of the one before it. [webvise uses this same boundary-first pattern](/#contact) when we design AI-assisted content and operations workflows for B2B teams.
How to create a profile
Begin from a Hermes setup that already works. Your provider, model, API keys, and default tools should be configured before you create specialists.

items: Create a research profile: `hermes profile create scout --clone`
Create a writing profile: `hermes profile create scribe --clone`
Create an engineering profile: `hermes profile create forge --clone`
Run a specialist directly: `hermes -p scout`, `hermes -p scribe`, or `hermes -p forge`

blocks.text: Use `--clone` when the base setup is already healthy. It copies useful setup files like config, environment, and SOUL.md, while the new profile still gets its own isolated memory and session history.
Use SOUL.md for identity and AGENTS.md for shared context
The profile name is not enough. If Scout, Scribe, and Forge all have the same SOUL.md, they are clones with labels.

SOUL.md should define the durable identity: tone, priorities, default behavior, strengths, and what the profile refuses to do. AGENTS.md should hold project context: repository structure, conventions, workflows, and tool rules.

rows: Role identity, taste, decision style, default standards
Temporary repo notes or client instructions
Project rules, file paths, commands, review process
Roster, handoffs, escalation rules, policy ceilings

blocks.text: A good Scout SOUL.md says: verify first, cite dates, separate evidence from inference, and flag uncertainty. A good Forge SOUL.md says: reproduce the failure, inspect logs, make the smallest safe change, and run the check again.
The day-30 checks matter more than the setup
Profiles look clean on day one. They blur on day 30 unless you audit drift, memory quality, cron ownership, and handoff shape.

items: **Profile drift:** diff each SOUL.md against its original version. New responsibilities need an explicit reason.
**Handoff rot:** store handoff rules in `~/.hermes/team/handoffs/`. Bad input should block the handoff, not merely warn.
**Memory rot:** run a weekly memory check per profile and resolve stale or contradictory notes before they become defaults.
**Cron collision:** keep one shared `~/.hermes/team/cron.md` so two profiles do not schedule competing jobs for the same outcome.

blocks.text: Hermes 0.12.0 added Curator for skill maintenance, which points at the broader rule: agent systems need housekeeping loops. Profiles reduce noise, but they do not remove the need to inspect what each role is learning.
A simple adoption path
Do not build a ten-agent org chart first. Create one specialist for the work that most pollutes your current assistant.

items: If research pollutes everything, create Scout first.
If drafts all sound like debug logs, create Scribe first.
If shell output keeps leaking into strategy work, create Forge first.
If messages, cron, and decisions are mixed together, keep Hermes as the orchestrator and move execution out.

blocks.text: The measure is not how many agents you have. The measure is whether each profile can get better at its job without making the other profiles worse.
